header:
Date: 2027-04-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Gomez (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Haven CTO), Mark Liu (Haven SRE), Evan Brooks (Haven ML)
summary: Deep dive on tail latency (p95/p99) for Haven's inference workloads. Main themes: KV cache warmup and misses, batching and queueing effects, streaming vs non-streaming RPC impacts, network hops (VPC peering/on-prem), quantization tradeoffs, and measurement methodology. Agreed next steps: share detailed buckets, Haven to provide payloads, Redwood to run sim and propose pilot plan.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we, uh, want to dig into the p99/p95 stuff you reported. can you give quick context on the workload?
[00:12] Priya: yeah thanks Alex, um so our inference endpoints are basically multi-tenant, mostly batched requests from robot fleets, average seq len ~180 tokens but heavy tail up to ~1k, we see p50 around 90ms p95 around 420ms and p99 spikes to 1.2s, which is what triggered this, right.
[00:36] Samir: okay got it. first question is measurement, are those numbers server-side only or end-to-end from client? any streaming involved?
[00:45] Mark: they're measured from our edge gateway (client -> edge -> redwood-hosted endpoint) so includes a couple network hops, and we are using non-streaming responses for now.
[00:55] Alex: non-streaming will often amplify tail — you end up buffering whole response, queueing — vs streaming where tokens start flowing earlier.
[01:05] Evan: question, we use a mix of hosted and some on-prem boxes, but most traffic hits hosted clusters in us-east, we also have north america robots hitting eu occasionally.
[01:18] Samir: that cross-region traffic explains a lot — network tail coupled with server-side tail. for p99 we split contributions: queuing + kernel (inference) + kv-cache misses + network. do you have logs with timing buckets?
[01:32] Priya: yes we have histograms, we'll share. few specifics: cache hit ratio on prefix cache is around 65% but drops during spike windows.
[01:40] Samir: a 35% miss rate can blow up p99 if cache miss forces full KV materialization per-request. our runtime keeps KV cache in-GPU when possible, but cold miss involves host->GPU transfer and kernel setup. those steps are expensive.
[01:55] Mark: is that the bulk transfer time? we saw stalls ~200-300ms on some misses.
[02:04] Alex: yeah that matches: host->device copies, followed by kernel startup, plus if quantized kernels need different code paths there's overhead. quantization can help throughput but sometimes hurts worst-case single-request latency if fallback to dequantize or different kernel occurs.
[02:20] Priya: we're using int8 quantized model for most traffic. we'd rather keep lower cost but worried about p99s.
[02:28] Samir: tradeoff: int8 paths give throughput and lower average but can add branching in runtime. we can tune per-route quantization profiles or use mixed precision for tail-sensitive routes.
[02:40] Evan: batching — we're currently batching up to 8 requests with a 40ms batch wait. could that create the tail?
[02:48] Samir: very likely. batching reduces avg token cost but adds headroom for queuing. p99 often dominated by either large batch queuing or serialized long-seq requests that fill GPU for many ms. do you have distribution of sequence lengths?
[03:02] Priya: yes most are 120-220 but around 2% exceed 600.
[03:07] Alex: that 2% will disproportionately affect p99. common mitigation: separate long-seq traffic into a different queue or model variant, or set max batch size that protects latency SLOs. also adaptive batching that favors latency SLOs over throughput during peaks.
[03:24] Mark: about network hops — we have edge -> internal LB -> redwood endpoint in a peered VPC, sometimes across regions. we rely on VPC peering and a transit gateway. any suggestions?
[03:36] Samir: reduce hops and keep streaming where possible. streaming reduces perceived latency because first tokens come earlier; also consider colocating cache or prefix cache closer to edge via CDN-like prefix caching, or enable TLS session reuse, keep-alive, and HTTP/2 multiplexing to reduce connection setup. peering and direct connect help a lot for determinism.
[03:56] Priya: security question — if we do Private (VPC) deployment, do we still get runtime-level KV cache in GPU or is it shared across nodes?
[04:05] Alex: For Private deployments we run the same runtime; cache is per-GPU instance but we have coordinated cache warmers and smart routing to hit nodes with warm caches when possible. dedicated capacity gives more predictable p99 since there's less noisy neighbor effects.
[04:20] Evan: what about autoscaling? we saw p99 spikes during autoscale events.
[04:25] Samir: autoscale can cause cold-start-like behaviors if new nodes aren't warmed — both the model and KV cache. recommended: warm replica pool, gradual rollout, and route long requests to warmed nodes. also can maintain small standby pool for burst traffic.
[04:40] Mark: measurement again — we want to break down p99 into components. is it possible to add per-request breakdown in Redwood console?
[04:48] Alex: yes we can surface token generation time, queue wait, KV miss time, network time (as measured at endpoint), and kernel time. it's not perfect but helps attribution. we'll share a sample dashboard.
[05:00] Priya: streaming vs non-streaming — we use non-streaming because our client assembly needs whole response, but maybe we can move to streaming for control plane messages. any pointers on how tokenization interacts with streaming?
[05:12] Samir: streaming sends early tokens; if you care about p99 for initial TTF (time-to-first-token) streaming helps a lot. for overall completion tail, long-seq requests still dominate. also be careful with HTTP chunking and client buffer behavior — some clients wait until buffer full before rendering, which defeats streaming benefits.
[05:32] Evan: there's also TLS termination at the edge causing some CPU time.
[05:36] Alex: right, move TLS termination closer to client or use HW TLS offload in edge to reduce latency.
[05:42] Priya: quantization tradeoffs — any quick heuristics? we saw small accuracy drop acceptable but p99 weirdness.
[05:50] Samir: try per-endpoint quantization profiles: keep fp16 for long-request or tail-sensitive endpoints, int8 for high-throughput short requests. also measure kernel switching cost: if runtime must swap kernels mid-batch that's bad. prefer homogenous batches per kernel type.
[06:05] Mark: what's our best immediate mitigation?
[06:08] Alex: short-term: separate long-seq traffic to dedicated route, reduce batch-wait for tail-sensitive route, enable streaming where possible. medium-term: tune KV cache warmers, prefetch common prefixes, and consider dedicated capacity or warmed standby. long-term: instrument fine-grained latency attribution and run controlled bench with your payloads.
[06:26] Evan: can you run a sim with our payloads and the 2% long-seq skew?
[06:30] Samir: yes we'll do that — action item.
[06:33] Priya: also we'd like to know cost delta if we move some routes to dedicated vs hosted.
[06:38] Alex: we'll include a rough cost arithmetic in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[06:42] (crosstalk)
[06:45] Alex: recap: Redwood shares spreadsheet + dashboard sample; Haven shares payloads + configs; Redwood runs sim and proposes pilot plan; schedule pilot kickoff next week.
[06:59] Mark: thanks all, that was useful.
[07:03] Alex: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email.
[07:06] — End of recording (note: timestamps in transcript are approximated; transcription contains minor errors)
